shaheen_chapter: Chapter 30: SCENES OF RAMALLAH THROUGH THE YEARS BY
caption: This picture dates from the turn of the century to show the beauty of the traditional Ramallah dress. The embroidered scarf she is wearing measures about one meter wide and two meters long. It was worn over the womanʼs head and came down to below her waist. The usual Ramallah colors of this hand embroidery were red and black. From about the 1930s and on this hand-embroidered scarf was replaced by a large machine-made shawl about one-and-a-half meters square that was folded in half to form a triangle and placed over the head to cover the upper part of the body. Until now, no woman who wears the traditional Ramallah costume will go outdoors without wearing this shawl. Both pictures on this page were taken from the volume Palestinian Costume by Shelagh Weir. In turn, both pictures are from the photo- graphic collection in the Library of Congress. Used by permission.
suggested_entry: Ramallah dress and embroidery

shaheen_chapter: Chapter 30: SCENES OF RAMALLAH THROUGH THE YEARS BY
caption: Two women inside their house, Ramallah, 1906. This is inside a turn-of-the-century house in Ramallah. In the background is the bedding placed in a niche in the wall. At night this bedding would be spread on the ﬂoor for the family to sleep on. The women are wearing the typical Ramallah costume of that time, which included the elaborate head piece with its two rows of coins. The upper row was known as the saffa and the lower row was called the shakka. Sometime around 1930 the saffa was dispensed with, and today only the shakka is worn. The embroidered scarf worn over the head piece, and which came down to below the womanʼs waist was not worn in the house but worn only when a woman went out of doors. The same is true of the heavily-embroidered jacket, the taqseereh. The women are wearing both indoors while they pose for this picture.

shaheen_chapter: Chapter 24: MOSES BAILEY
caption: A picture of the orchards and ﬁelds, no doubt in the Ramallah area, as they appeared in 1920. The main object of this picture is the building in the center, but it cannot be identiﬁed. It is too large to be a local shrine, known as a maqam or a qubbeh. A maqam was a small room generally built in an open area over the grave of a holy man. There the local inhabitants would go and make various requests, as offer prayers for the safety or healing of a member of their family or, if a woman was unable to conceive, to be healed of her barrenness. A piece of an old garment of the one praying would then be tied to a nearby tree so that the saint invoked would remember that personʼs prayer. But the building in this picture is much too large to be a maqam, although these shrines were generally built in a similar setting in open ﬁelds.

shaheen_chapter: Chapter 12: THE FAMILY OF SALEM BUTROS JABER
caption: Coming out of the church in the old part of the city of Ramallah after the wedding of Ramzi and Nahida Jaber, April 19, 1953. But that old style of building with thick stone walls in which the walls inside the house arch to a point in the middle of the ceiling, called ‘aked architecture in Arabic, keeps the house cool in summer and warm in winter. The tree top in the upper right is where the Greek Orthodox Church is located. That tree was cut down in 2002 when the church building was expanded to include a new bell tower and ofﬁces to house a Greek Orthodox Patriarchate, an extension of the Patriarchate in Jerusalem.

caption: The priest (el-Khoury) Hanna Jubran of the Shakara clan, the father of Badi‘a Khoury. He was born in 1865 and died 1924. He served as a priest in Jaffa, Lydda, Ramleh, Gaza, and in el-Salt, which is in Jordan. Most of his ministry was in Jaffa; he would come to Ramallah only during feast days. shaheen_chapter: Chapter 28: MANARA SQUARE
caption: A sketch of the original cast iron structure that stood in the center of Manara Square from about 1934-1950. Electricity ﬁrst came to Ramallah in 1934 when the Brit- ish authorities built this electical distribution structure in the center of the Square. About 8 feet high and 10 feet across, it rested upon a stone foundation of two steps. Manara Square got its name from the bright light on the roof of the structure that illuminated the Square at night. Those who remember the structure recall that the globe enclosing the light was “as large as a small watermelon.” (Sketch by Mr. Hosni Radwan.)
